podcasts.title: How To Build The Future: Paul Graham & Amjad Masad
podcasts.description: Replit was building toward the AI coding era years before it had a name. In 2024, the company shipped an agent that could take a request in plain English, work through errors, provision its own infrastructure, and keep going until the software actually worked. The model companies even reached out to ask how Replit had pulled it off.Co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad had been thinking about making programming radically more accessible since 2008, and Replit’s original pitch deck predicted AI-generated code before the Transformer paper was published. Today, that same technology is moving into banks, manufacturers, and other large companies, where Amjad says teams are replacing software projects once scoped at $10 million with $250,000 of Replit.On How to Build the Future, Paul Graham sits down with Amjad to talk about why Replit was so well positioned when coding agents arrived, what comes after vibe coding, and his bigger vision for the “self-driving company,” where AI agents increasingly build and operate the software a company needs.

podcasts.title: America Votes Against Data Centers, Implications for Big Tech and Beyond, Were Google Bears Right All Along?
podcasts.description: Ben and Andrew begin with reactions to this week’s elections and their implications across tech. First: The resounding rejection of AI data centers in localities across the country, why a pause in Texas is particularly problematic for U.S. AI infrastructure, widespread resentment of big tech, and the big tech blind spots that led to this point. From there: A digression SpaceX and data centers in space, why hyperscalers figure to be the beneficiaries of a buildout bottleneck, and a word about China. At the end: A Google state of the union after last week’s earnings, Reddit scrambles to adapt to a new environment, and AI Show & Tell spawns a discussion about the group chat era of software.

podcasts.title: Ramtin Naimi - The State of Venture - [Invest Like the Best, EP.499]
podcasts.description:
My guest today is Ramtin Naimi, the founder of Abstract Ventures, back for our second conversation. Few people see as many companies as Ramtin and his firm, so this time we zoom in on what they’re seeing right now.

The question he keeps coming back to is whether this is 2019 or 2021: early in a run, or at the top of one. Hot rounds now come with a second, pricier tranche for the firms that lost the deal, and he’s seen more term sheets pulled or renegotiated in recent weeks than at any time since 2021.

We also get into the neolabs, one of which plans to spend $1 billion on a single training run, how the goalposts for a best-case outcome moved from $10 billion to a trillion dollars, and the biggest mistake he’s made building Abstract.

Please enjoy my conversation with Ramtin Naimi.

podcasts.title: Ep. 043 - The Midterms and the 2028 Datacenter Buildout (Datacenters) | Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros, Jordan Nanos, Maya Barkin, Wayne Ma
podcasts.description:
Recorded Election Day morning, before any results: SemiAnalysis’s model has about 62 GW of US datacenter additions in 2028, most not yet under construction and sitting in states electing a governor. Texas alone is close to 30%.

Jordan Nanos (@JordanNanos) sits down with Maya Barkin (@mayabarkin), Wayne Ma (@waynema) and Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros (@JeremieEO) on why 2027 is largely locked in, why the backlash crosses party lines, and how developers can win over their neighbors.

Since recording: the AP called Texas for Gina Hinojosa, who would pause datacenter permitting, and Georgia for Keisha Lance Bottoms, and Democrats took a 3-2 majority on Georgia’s Public Service Commission, which sets power rates. (As of Nov 4, 2:35 PM ET.)
